title: Skin lumps — care navigation summary
content: Project-authored summary based on MedlinePlus: an unexplained lump or swelling should be assessed by a health professional rather than treated at home without a diagnosis. Useful details include location, when it began, pain, growth, bleeding or drainage, number of lumps, appearance, and other symptoms. An examination may be followed by imaging or sampling when the cause is unclear. A chat description cannot establish whether a lump is harmless or serious.

title: Coughing up blood — urgent care navigation summary
content: Project-authored summary based on MedlinePlus: coughing up blood or bloody mucus from the respiratory tract should be medically assessed even when no other symptom is present. Track the duration, frequency, approximate amount, and whether the blood is streaked through mucus. Get medical help right away for more than a few teaspoons, bleeding that will not stop, chest pain, dizziness or lightheadedness, fever, or severe shortness of breath. Blood-thinning medicines and other medicines are important details for the clinician.

title: Traditional Chinese medicine — evidence and safety summary
publisher: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
license: U.S. government public domain unless marked
content: Project-authored summary based on NCCIH: evidence varies across traditional Chinese medicine practices. Some research supports selected uses of acupuncture or tai chi, while studies of Chinese herbal products have mixed results. Safety problems reported for some products include undeclared ingredients, substitution, contamination, heavy metals, pesticides, and organ toxicity. Acupuncture should be delivered by a properly qualified practitioner using appropriate sterile technique.

title: Herb–medicine interactions — clinical caution summary
publisher: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
license: U.S. government public domain unless marked
content: Project-authored summary based on NCCIH: herbal products can have pharmacologic effects, direct toxicities, contaminants, and interactions with prescription or over-the-counter medicines. Evidence for many suspected interactions remains limited or indirect, so uncertainty should be stated. Extra caution is warranted with medicines that have a narrow therapeutic index, anticoagulants, chemotherapy, transplant medicines, digoxin, and around surgery, pregnancy, or liver and kidney disease. A pharmacist or doctor should review the exact product and medication list.

title: Evidence-based traditional and integrative medicine policy
content: Project-authored policy summary: the WHO Traditional Medicine Strategy 2025–2034 emphasizes strengthening the evidence base, safety, effectiveness, appropriate regulation, qualified practice, and responsible integration into health systems. Inclusion of a traditional practice or classification is not proof that a specific intervention is effective. Patient-facing answers should distinguish cultural or traditional frameworks from evidence about benefits and harms.

title: Singapore Chinese proprietary medicine safeguards
content: Project-authored regulatory summary based on HSA: Chinese proprietary medicines sold in Singapore are subject to product-listing and dealer requirements, ingredient restrictions, contaminant limits, and labelling rules. The required sale statement advises consumer discretion. Consumers should use reputable sources, check current HSA information, and consult a registered TCM practitioner plus a pharmacist or doctor when medicines, pregnancy, surgery, allergies, or chronic disease could change risk.
